metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Monongah, WV
metaDescription: Monongah, Marion County mineral owners: 1907 mining-disaster era heirship, legacy Big Injun wells, and multi-generation fractional interests.
heroLead: Monongah's mineral title history is inseparable from the 1907 mining disaster that scattered families and left many estates unsettled for generations.
intro: The 1907 Monongah mine explosion, one of the deadliest in American history, left the town with an unusual number of estates that passed through sudden, unplanned inheritance rather than an orderly transfer. More than a century later, that history still shows up in Marion County deed books as mineral interests tied to those original, often-unprobated estates.

sections.heading: Estates rooted in the 1907 disaster
paragraphs: When a mineral-owning family lost its head of household suddenly and without a will, the estate often stayed informally divided among surviving relatives rather than going through a formal probate — especially in an era when the mineral interest wasn't seen as particularly valuable. Those same interests, now under Marcellus-adjacent acreage, can carry a dozen or more current heirs tracing back to that single unresolved estate.

sections.heading: Legacy wells and current corridor development
paragraphs: Monongah sits close to Marion County's Route 250 development corridor, and Big Injun and Gordon sand wellbores from earlier drilling eras remain present on some tracts alongside newer Marcellus leasing. Confirming which lease and which formation actually governs your interest is the first step before any sale.

sections.heading: What a records search actually turns up for Monongah families
paragraphs: A courthouse records search for a Monongah-area family name often turns up more than one mineral interest tied to different tracts, since coal-camp era families frequently held small pieces of land in several nearby locations rather than one consolidated farm. It's common for an heir to be surprised at how many separate interests come back under a single surname search.
Sorting out which interests are actually yours to sell — versus a cousin's or a more distant relative's branch of the family — is part of the title work we do before making an offer.

faqs.question: Does the 1907 disaster still affect mineral title in Monongah today?
faqs.answer: In a real, practical sense — many estates from that era were never formally probated, which means current heirs sometimes discover an interest through a records search rather than a will.

faqs.question: How do I document my share of an interest tracing back that far?
faqs.answer: An heirship affidavit supported by whatever family records exist (death certificates, prior deeds, family Bibles with recorded births/deaths) can establish your claim; a courthouse title check confirms the deed chain.

faqs.question: Is Monongah near active Marcellus development?
faqs.answer: Yes, it's close to Marion County's Route 250 corridor, where horizontal units have been developed on surrounding acreage.

faqs.question: What if a title search turns up interests I didn't know my family held?
faqs.answer: That happens fairly often here given the area's history. Each interest can be reviewed and, if documented, sold or retained on its own.
